How Love Saves Lives

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When someone takes his own life, the grief of parents, lovers, children, and friends can be unspeakable.
  • How could this talented, beautiful young person not know she’d be terribly, horribly missed?
  • Most experts attribute suicide to severe mental illness caused by a brain injury or genetic predisposition, or due to some other, as yet unknown, physical or chemical trigger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When someone takes his own life, the grief of parents, lovers, children, and friends can be unspeakable. At a memorial for one young suicide I attended a few years ago, the father of the deceased could barely walk to the altar to light a candle. Everyone was crying.

How could this talented, beautiful young person not know she’d be terribly, horribly missed?

Most experts attribute suicide to severe mental illness caused by a brain injury or genetic predisposition, or due to some other, as yet unknown, physical or chemical trigger. Severe depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia are all inordinately common among people who die by suicide.

Severe mental illnesses are no doubt responsible for many, if not most, of the eight hundred thousand or so suicides that occur around the world each year, including, perhaps, that young person’s whose memorial I attended.

It has been revealed that my book, Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic, isn’t primarily about such cases—or about how to prevent suicide. Such a book would have detailed sections about psychotherapy, restrictions on firearms, safety barriers for bridges, and other measures that really do save lives. Instead, my aim was to explore why some people want to take their own lives in the first place and how that desire might be reduced, in both individuals and communities.

Having spent the past few years reading about suicide, speaking with scores of people who’ve experienced suicidal feelings, and having experienced them myself from time to time, I’ve come to understand that what suicidal people feel is the indifference, not of the universe, but of those closest to them. They sense that their own feelings don’t matter to the people they care most about.

These experiences are backed up by studies showing that the main reason suicidal people want to die is because they think no one cares about them. Some suicides even seem to believe they’re doing everyone a favor by taking their own lives.

Psychologist Thomas Joiner, who’s been studying suicide for thirty years, calls it a force of nature that distorts people’s minds so they become convinced that they are a burden to others and no one wants them around. In study after study, the most common trigger for suicide is a perceived rupture in a close relationship, either with a lover, parent, or other close relative, that seems irreparable to the suicidal person.

Given that suicide seems driven by fraught or broken connections, it’s perhaps not surprising that I also discovered that suicide can spread within social groups like a disease. The suicide rate of particular groups can jump—sometimes increasing three- or four-fold or more—in a short time, meaning it behaves like an epidemic, like malaria during the rainy season or flu in the fall. Suicide epidemics unfold more slowly than these microbial plagues—over years or decades, not weeks or months—but they happen far too rapidly to result from genetic changes, and affect far too many people to be explained away as spontaneous cases of biologically caused mental illness or brain injury. The causes therefore must have something to do with the changing social environment in which these people live. Suicide epidemics have occurred on virtually every continent.

Recent findings suggest that what’s scary about this is that it means suicide could come for any of us. The very existence of suicide epidemics proves that people with suicidal feelings aren’t a species apart. Anyone can feel suicidal under certain conditions—and the key to stopping suicide epidemics is to change those conditions.

In a recent development, I teach and write about public health and have long been fascinated by epidemics because they always tell a story. In most literary depictions of epidemics, such as Albert Camus’s The Plague or Daniel Defoe’s A Journal of the Plague Year, they seem to strike from nowhere, but this isn’t how epidemics typically behave. Individual cases of disease are hard to predict. Some of us will become ill tomorrow, but there’s no telling who. Even those who take risks may well escape the consequences.

What might cause a suicide epidemic?

Industry observers note that first, it’s notable to understand what doesn’t. Suicide isn’t more common during wars or where people are poorer or have recently experienced some environmental disaster like a flood, earthquake, or wildfire. Suicide was common among African slaves, especially on the ships en route to America and when they first arrived, but despite segregation, police brutality, mass incarceration, and other outrages, the suicide rate of African Americans has been generally lower than that of U.S. whites since record-keeping began in the 1930s.

What seems to matter is whether people believe someone, somewhere, really cares about and understands them.

The mental pain that drives suicide is really the flip side of love, says Israeli neuroscientist Yoram Yovell. “It probably evolved along with motherhood. . . . Inherent in us are very strong emotional forces that function to keep mothers and babies together. When they get too far from each other, they feel mental pain,” which we experience when we search for love. This is why “so many children’s stories are about a boy looking for his lost mother.”.

Evidence supports Yovell’s theory. A 1999 study found that some 78% of high lethality suicide attempters had recently experienced the loss of a close personal relationship, and suicide notes often express love for those left behind. In 2012, Zimri Yaseen and his colleagues reported that suicidal people interviewed in emergency rooms were especially likely to report that in the three preceding days, they’d felt “unusually intense or deep feelings of love,” which they presumably also felt were not reciprocated.

Recent findings suggest that but why would large groups of people—from the islands of Micronesia to the Arctic Circle, from the cities of post-communist Russia to the towns of contemporary America—suddenly begin questioning their most intimate attachments? How does love suddenly disappear—or seem to—from the lives of thousands of people?

In my book, Why Live, I argue that it has to do with how we internalize socioeconomic change.

Industry observers note that the first well-researched suicide epidemic occurred across Western Europe during the 19th century. Intellectuals debated the causes as we debate the vicissitudes of the stock market. Rising suicide rates were attributed to socialism, atmospheric moisture, the vice of masturbation, and the Romantic era inclination to preserve—through death—the passions of youth against the onslaught of Bourgeois boredom brought on by industrialization and urban life.

Recent findings suggest that doctors even searched, in vain, for a “suicidogenic” organ in the cadavers of people who’d died by suicide. But others blamed society, that collective property of human groups that shapes our thinking and behavior.

As a Jew growing up in France amid increasing anti-Semitism, Émile Durkheim had seen how shared values and beliefs buffered his people against the effects of discrimination and how anti-Semitism tightened bonds among them. He went on to become one of the founders of sociology, which is the study of those bonds: what holds us together, what drives us apart, and what happens as a result.

According to recent reports, in his 1897 book, Suicide, Durkheim theorized that suicides increase wherever society is fragmenting and people are growing more detached from one another: where divorce rates are higher, for example, and where Protestants, with their individualistic culture and aloofness from collective ritual, outnumber Catholics. He likened it to entropy—the universal tendency toward chaos and disorder at the atomic level discovered by physicists earlier in the century. Appearing on the eve of humanity’s, as yet, bloodiest century, Durkheim’s book seemed to foreshadow the trouble to come.

What is it about fragmenting societies that causes mental pain?

Durkheim was vague, even a little loopy, when it came to explaining this. At the time, psychologists were just discovering the unconscious, which they explored through studies of hypnosis and hallucinations. Durkheim followed this research closely, and believed that values and meanings flowed through populations like electrical currents, as if societies had what scholars Laurent Mucchielli and Marc Renneville refer to as a “collective soul.” These currents could change people’s behavior through unconscious mechanisms, just as changes in temperature and pressure change the behavior of molecules.

Industry observers note that many late-19th-century scientists believed that our brains generated signals analogous to radio waves. Alexander Graham Bell, Nikola Tesla, and James Clerk Maxwell even wired up helmets and other gizmos to try to measure them. Mark Twain told Harper’s Monthly that thoughts could shoot from brain to brain, without their owners having to open their mouths to communicate. Likewise, Durkheim maintained that whatever suicidal people stated about their feelings were just expressions of resolutions planted in their minds by the vibes of a disintegrating society.

Industry observers note that the brain-wave theory eventually fell out of fashion. In the 1930s, one of Durkheim’s protégés came closer to explaining the psychological effects of social fragmentation. Maurice Halbwachs taught at the University of Strasbourg from 1919 until his death in a Nazi concentration camp in 1945. His 1930 monograph The Causes of Suicide identified an existential loneliness that, if not entirely fresh, flourished in the growing towns and cities of 19th-century Europe and the countryside they engulfed.

According to Halbwachs, cities create opportunities for social and economic advancement, but they also create the conditions for exploitative relationships, swindles, romantic betrayals, fragile friendships, broken families, unstable jobs, and many other sources of despair.

As European cities grew, so did a latest class of people who were particularly prone to suicide, including abandoned lovers, lonely widowers, workers who’d lost their jobs, nobles shamed by some dishonorable act, gamblers who couldn’t pay their debts, merchants who’d ruined themselves, heirs who’d squandered their fortunes, and others who’d suffered a common bitter fate: sudden exclusion from a cherished social community. As Halwachs writes:.

They all see their social level lowered. They are to a certain extent declassed. But what does it mean to be declassed? It is to pass from a group that one knows, that esteems you, to another that ignores you and whose appreciation one has no reason to hold. One then feels a void opening around oneself. Those who once surrounded you, with whom you had so many ideas in common, so many prejudices in common, with whom so many affinities brought you together because you found yourself in them as they found yourself in you, suddenly move away. You disappear from their concerns and their memory. Those among whom you find yourself understand neither your disorientation, nor your nostalgia and your regrets. Detached from the group by a sudden shock, you are incapable, or at least you believe yourself incapable, of ever finding in another any support, nor anything to replace what you have lost.

Sources indicate that in the midst of the 19th-century suicide crisis, the very meaning of the word “lonely” changed, from an adjective typically used to describe empty places and people who stood alone before God to one with the emotional and psychological connotations it has for us today. Suicidal despair, Halbwachs wrote, had been rarer in the past because traditional rural life was simpler and more predictable:.

We lived on the spot . . . adapted to each other, knowing each other too well to be frequently exposed to the clashes that occur when we move from one place, one situation, one profession, to another. Business carried less risk. Ambitions were less aroused, humiliations rarer. We thought and felt in common. Sorrows and troubles, instead of concentrating within the consciousness of this or that individual, dispersed and died out within the group.

What Halbwachs was describing was the transition from what German sociologist Ferdinand Tönnies called Gemeinschaft, or communities based on trust, mutual respect, and sharing of whatever material goods one had, to Gesellschaft, societies based largely on market transactions and political calculation in which ties of friendship and loyalty are relegated to private family life, and may not even reliably be found there.

As far as I’ve been able to determine, wherever that transition has occurred, a suicide epidemic has followed swiftly behind.

In a recent development, but there is another ingredient, too. As villagers shifted away from subsistence and small-scale farming to wage labor and trade, their intimate relationships became both more fragile and more precious. The extended family, which once formed a social mesh that supported everyone, waned in significance, and walls rose up around increasingly private and nuclearized families, usually dominated by a single, generally male breadwinner, upon whom everyone else in the family depended. If you felt your family didn’t respect and care about you, you were in a latest sort of trouble, not just because the community no longer offered you a livelihood, but because your whole identity was at stake.

Sources indicate that modern capitalist society creates, in all of us, something of the double consciousness described by the great African American sociologist W. E. B. DuBois. When a modern person looks at a stranger, he wonders not only, as his villager ancestors did, “What can I do to help this person? And is he the kind of person who will help me?” but “What does that stranger see when he looks at me? What essence does he detect? A beauty or a beast? A success or a failure? A respectable person or a fool?”.

Recent findings suggest that the answer sometimes comes as a disappointment. In traditionally cohesive societies, this mattered less, because a person’s worth was measured by what he did for others, and everyone was capable of contributing something. You might not be the best hunter, fisherman, storyteller, or drummer; you might not be the best grower of breadfruit or builder of igloos; but you still mattered. Only the greedy and selfish were looked down upon and excluded.

According to recent reports, in modern societies, generosity still counts, but for far less than it used to. If others find us wanting—because of our looks, talents, graces, bank accounts, intelligence, or for whatever reason—we are alone with it, and must make sense of it, somehow.

For most of us, what makes modern life, with all its loneliness and insecurity, bearable are close relationships with people we count on to see and accept us for who we really are—whatever our flaws. Romantic rejection is exquisitely painful because we feel that that special quality within us, the thing that makes us lovable—and everyone has something—has either been unrecognized or, worse, seen and rejected.

The pain of rejection by a parent or other close relative is even worse because it can make us feel as though no one could ever understand and sympathize with us. After all, they know us best of all.

In the absence of an abstract sense of group belonging, interpersonal love, especially between parents and children and romantic partners, has become the main source of our psychological resilience, our ability to withstand the disappointments encountered in the outside world, just as the mutually reinforcing group gave strength to our ancestors fighting for survival on the plains, tundras, beaches, and forests of the past.

Love is not just a feeling; it’s also a culture, which developed fairly recently, first in Western societies, and then around the world on the heels of capitalism, modernity, and individualism. It’s no coincidence, the social philosopher Erich Fromm pointed out, that as modern ways of life displaced the traditional, cohesive village and clan, love poems, songs, and stories came to occupy the center of Western culture, displacing archaic tales of heroism and godliness.

In a recent development, it’s not that love was absent from the art of the ancient past, but as often as not, it was seen as a cause of calamity and human folly. Think of Helen of Troy, Dido and Aeneas, Adam and Eve. Then, more or less in lockstep with commercial culture and urbanization, love came to be seen as a force superior to the gods or God or honor or historic destiny.

The behavior of parents and spouses changed, too. Until the 1800s, childrearing in England, for example, was seen as an exercise less in nurturing than in training for adulthood. Men who were fed up with their wives could sell them at markets or abandon them and marry someone else without divorcing. Infants who died weren’t even listed in parish registers. Only in the 19th century did heartfelt observations of sons and daughters begin appearing regularly in the diaries of American and English mothers.

Recent findings suggest that with the growth of markets and formal state institutions, people came to rely less on kinship networks for social welfare and trade and the family gradually shifted from an economic enterprise to a child-centered haven in a heartless world. The 1700s saw the first toy shops, women’s magazines, popular child care manuals, and family portraits. Christian churches, which had previously stressed family discipline and sometimes even the virtues of wife-beating, now promoted ideals of conjugal and parental love.

Today, birthday parties, children’s allowances, and Valentine’s Day cards are symbols we use to assure each other that our most important relationships are real. Meanwhile, parenting manuals, happily-ever-after fairy tales, Hollywood movies, and the novels of Jane Austen, George Eliot, Charles Dickens, Barbara Cartland, Colleen Hoover, and countless others illustrate the enactment of love according to Western norms.

Sources indicate that premodern Europeans, as well as Indigenous groups the world over, didn’t need this culture because in the mutual aid communities of bygone days, you knew who you were and what you needed to do to gain the esteem of others: You had to pitch in for the group. You helped others and they helped you. That was love, and according to accounts of anthropologists, it was everywhere, as ubiquitous as air.

Sources indicate that but when these groups modernized, in some cases very rapidly under the forces of capitalism and colonialism, the rules changed. Now it was unclear what the common goals were and what others were looking for in us. If they didn’t like us, there wasn’t a lot we could do about it. If the people we loved—our romantic partners, parents, and children—felt that way, it was intolerably painful because our hearts had nowhere to turn. Every rejection could now elicit devastating feelings of aloneness. “Who am I?” we are left to wonder. “Am I worth anything at all to anyone?”.

In a recent development, signifiers of love—birthday cards and so on—aren’t enough. We need the confidence that our own feelings are understood. Some people, either because of the distortions of mental illness or because they really are lost and alone, simply don’t have it.

According to recent reports, but all is not lost. As I argue in Why Live, communities can regrow, just like decimated forests. The best policy I can think of is to strive for greater economic equality, which will naturally reduce insecurity, and, in turn, foster greater spiritual as well as material generosity. We are kinder to one another when we don’t feel threatened. Otherwise, the best advice I can think of is not to make things worse. When positive communities begin to emerge, the trick is not to ruin them.

In a recent development, let’s treat communities like ecosystems so that every time a major economic policy shift is proposed—a massive fresh trade deal or development project—the effects on communities are considered, and the preservation of Gemeinschaft is prioritized. Ideally, studies of this, analogous to the environmental impact studies now required by all World Bank loans to developing countries, would be conducted with the full and meaningful involvement of affected communities.

Sources indicate that some elements of Gemeinschaft survive, even in these harsh times—in well-functioning neighborhoods, in friendship networks, sometimes in the military, and in some schools and workplaces. You know it when you see it; it’s where you feel your dignity is recognized. In defending and building that, we give everyone more reason to live.

Helen C. Epstein, Ph.D., is visiting professor of global public health and human rights at Bard College. She is the author of Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic and Another Fine Mess: America, Uganda, and the War on Terror.

How to Start a Side Business While Working Full-Time

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Recent findings suggest that the number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy.
  • Validation does not require a perfect product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that the number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you strategy to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Sources indicate that forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as swiftly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Sources indicate that side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

According to recent reports, one of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Organization). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

Industry observers note that an LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Recent findings suggest that self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

It has been revealed that quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

Industry observers note that ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

$95 annual fee | Earn 75,000 bonus points.

Side hustlers! With the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card you can earn free travel from your business expenses.

In a recent development, chooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

It has been revealed that the biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

In a recent development, the 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

Industry observers note that the FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice claims to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

In a recent development, the decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the key thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Industry observers note that pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

In a recent development, create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Sources indicate that once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and firm handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Industry observers note that most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

In a recent development, businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

According to recent reports, start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Recent findings suggest that starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP swiftly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

The State With The Most Wendy's Locations Isn't New York, California, Or Texas

  • The Sunshine State accounts for roughly 8% of the total number of locations this fast food giant has in the United States, compared to Texas, which has slightly fewer locations at 419.
  • Sources indicate that additionally, two Florida cities — Miami and Orlando — are in the top five U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wendy's is a beloved chain of fast food restaurants whose square-shaped burger patties are instantly recognizable to many American diners. Founded in 1969 in Columbus, Ohio, the brand is an institution where it was born — yet the Midwestern state doesn't actually have the most locations. Neither do populous hubs like California or New York. Rather, you need to look southeast to the land of orange groves. With 464 restaurants as of November 2026, Florida has more Wendy's locations than any other state in the country.

The Sunshine State accounts for roughly 8% of the total number of locations this fast food giant has in the United States, compared to Texas, which has slightly fewer locations at 419. However, if you take population differences into account, there are more restaurants per capita in Florida than in the Lone Star State. This means that Florida residents are more likely to find a Wendy's nearby. Not everything seems to be bigger in Texas, after all, at least when it comes to this fast food chain.

Sources indicate that additionally, two Florida cities — Miami and Orlando — are in the top five U.S. cities with the most Wendy's locations (per ScrapeHero). So, whether you're enjoying the nightlife of South Beach or visiting Disney World, you won't be too far from a Jr. Bacon Cheeseburger. Despite Florida's distinction of having the most locations, however, it doesn't have the largest Wendy's in the world. That honor goes to Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, a country in the Caucasus region.

It has been revealed that the idea of people vacationing in, moving to, or spending part of the year in Florida is an old trope, and there's a good reason for it. Many Americans see the state as a respite from the cold, and the Sunshine State actually has a long history of being a destination for migrants moving down from northern states, dating back to as early as the 1800s.

Interestingly, people from Ohio comprise a large portion of these migrants — in fact, according to USAFacts, more Ohioans moved to Florida than to any other state in 2024. Just like immigrants from other countries, American transplants bring their own cultures that can influence the local culinary scene, and maybe that's why there are so many Wendy's locations in the Sunshine State.

Considering how the brand was founded in the Buckeye State, perhaps the many transplants brought their taste for the chain's iconic baked potatoes, chili, and square burgers with them. After all, Ohio has the third-largest number of Wendy's restaurants and has more locations per capita than Florida. It might seem like mere coincidence until you take into account the fact that Florida is also home to another Buckeye institution, Skyline Chili, and it's the only state outside the Midwest where the chain is present.

Crostata Di Mele (Italian Apple Pie) Recipe

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while working as a young pastry chef in an Italian trattoria, I had the great fortune of spending 3 weeks eating my way through Italy in an attempt to discover the most unique and tempting desserts each region had to offer.
  • My recipe for crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is a bakery-worthy homage to those delightful desserts, and it became a seasonal fixture on my pastry menu.
  • Learning how to make the dough and filling for this crostata will give you a solid foundation for making other Italian pastries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while working as a young pastry chef in an Italian trattoria, I had the great fortune of spending 3 weeks eating my way through Italy in an attempt to discover the most unique and tempting desserts each region had to offer. Although I tasted complex and ethereal cakes, pastries, and frozen delights, I kept coming back to the simple fruit crostatas: buttery crusts molded into tart pans or baked free-form in rustic rounds, topped with glistening fruits and cakey or custardy fillings. These desserts tasted like perfection in their simplicity and purity of flavors.

My recipe for crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is a bakery-worthy homage to those delightful desserts, and it became a seasonal fixture on my pastry menu. A traditional pasta frolla (Italian short dough) crust is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere (pastry cream custard) and topped with tart, crisp apples and crunchy turbinado sugar. The warm crostata is given a finishing glaze of melted apricot preserves, then chilled for serving.

Learning how to make the dough and filling for this crostata will give you a solid foundation for making other Italian pastries. The dough is easy to work with, and the pastry cream is a versatile filling for other treats, such as profiteroles, layer cakes, or napoleons.

Industry observers note that there are 3 main components in the crostata di mele: the crust, the custard filling, and the toppings. For the crust, you will need all-purpose flour, granulated sugar, sea salt, cold unsalted butter, a large egg plus 1 yolk, vanilla extract, and the zest of a large lemon. The difference between this crostata dough and regular apple pie dough is the addition of eggs, which makes the dough slightly less flaky but more pliable for rolling and shaping. For the pastry cream, you will need whole milk, a vanilla bean, more lemon zest, 4 yolks, granulated sugar, and cornstarch. You will split the vanilla bean lengthwise to release the tiny black seeds into the milk, and the cornstarch acts as a thickening agent. To top the crostata, I like using apples that are crisp and tart, but that also have a balance of sweetness. Honeycrisp, Pink Lady, and Granny Smith are perfect apple varieties for this recipe. You will toss your apple slices with fresh lemon juice to prevent browning before baking, and use some melted butter to secure a crunchy sprinkling of turbinado sugar. To give your baked crostata a shiny finish, you will need apricot preserves to melt down and strain.

Combine the flour, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.

Add the butter a few pieces at a time and mix until pea-sized clumps form.

Add the egg, yolk, lemon zest, and vanilla, and mix until a dough forms.

Shape the dough into a disk, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes.

While the dough is chilling, heat the milk, vanilla bean, and lemon zest strips in a medium saucepan until it barely starts to simmer.

Remove the pan from the heat, cover, and steep for 10 minutes.

Place a medium glass bowl on a damp kitchen towel or mat to prevent slipping.

Add the egg yolks, sugar, and cornstarch and whisk until thick and pale yellow.

Remove the vanilla bean and zest strips with a slotted spoon, then discard.

Gradually add the warm milk to the egg mixture, whisking constantly.

In a recent development, transfer the mixture back to the saucepan and cook over low heat, stirring frequently until it comes to a boil. Turn the heat to low and whisk constantly for 1 minute.

In a recent development, remove the pan from the heat, then scrape the filling into a heat-proof bowl and press a piece of plastic wrap to the surface. Chill for at least 2 hours.

In a large bowl, toss the apple slices with the lemon juice.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Press the dough into the pan and trim the excess flush with the edge of the pan.

Spread the cooled pastry cream evenly over the bottom of the pastry shell.

Arrange the slices in concentric overlapping circles over the pastry cream, starting from the outer edge and working inward.

Brush the apples with the melted butter and sprinkle on the turbinado sugar.

Bake the crostata di mele for about 50 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the apples are tender.

While the crostata is baking, heat the apricot jam with 1 tablespoon of water in a small saucepan until warm and liquid.

Strain the jam if any large pieces of fruit remain.

Remove the crostata from the oven and immediately brush on the apricot glaze.

Cool the crostata completely in the pan on a rack before removing from the pan.

Slice the crostata and serve at room temperature or chilled.

Our bakery-worthy crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere and topped with tart, crisp apples.

In a recent development, the crostata is one of the most continuously made dessert forms found in Italian baking, dating back to the 1400s. Not only is the crostata found in pastry shops and on restaurant menus, but it is also the one dessert that many people make at home with whatever ingredients are on hand. This kind of humble tart was likely consumed at breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Sources indicate that the crostata di mele probably originated in northern Italy, where apples are grown in abundance. In order to highlight the fresh flavor of the apples, crostata de mele is spiced with a light hand. Subtle cinnamon and a hint of nutmeg might be used, along with the zest of a lemon, as in this recipe. With only a few simple ingredients, the recipe is also dependent on using a light hand in preparation. The dough should be minimally handled to prevent a tough or shrunken crust. The pastry cream must be carefully tempered to prevent lumps from forming. And nothing should get in the way of the apples being the star.

Even though there may seem to be a lot of steps to this recipe, there are lots of ways to do advance prep to save time. First, your crostata dough can be mixed, shaped into a disk, wrapped, and chilled for several days in the refrigerator. You can also freeze this dough for up to 3 months. Once you are ready to roll out the dough, allow it to come to cool to room temperature before you shape it. You can also roll out and fill your tart pan, then wrap the unbaked shell and refrigerate or freeze until it is time to fill and bake.

Industry observers note that the pastry cream should only be made 1 or 2 days in advance, and this custardy filling should not be frozen unless it is layered into a dessert (too much separation will occur). Wait until just before baking to spread the pastry cream into your tart shell so that the dough will not become soggy.

It has been revealed that from experience, I know that this crostata di mele will stay fresh, tasty, and sliceable for almost a week under refrigeration. That said, it is crucial to always keep the crostata chilled to prevent bacterial growth in the custard layer. Typically, 3-5 days is the best range for serving this dessert.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that derived from Mexican and Tejano cooking methods, Tex-Mex was born out of a meeting of cultures that combined time-honored techniques and upcoming ingredients.
  • Flour tortillas and dairy, like cheddar and Colby jack cheeses, are also major parts of the Tex-Mex food culture, as are queso dips and customizable combinations of rice, beans, proteins, and cheeses in a personal-sized bowl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tex-Mex food is incredibly popular across the country, but the line between it and more traditional Mexican fare can be a bit hard to define. Plus, there are other offshoots, like California or Upcoming Mexican styles that overlap with Tex-Mex but use different ingredients, such as avocados or hatch chiles. To cut down on some of the confusion, we've created this list to help you find the most reliable, tasty, and distinctly Tex-Mex quick service and casual restaurant chains you can dine at, according to the people who eat at them.

Sources indicate that derived from Mexican and Tejano cooking methods, Tex-Mex was born out of a meeting of cultures that combined time-honored techniques and upcoming ingredients. For instance, cumin and dried chili powder had recently become available, and they quickly caught on in Tex-Mex cooking. Now the pungent, earthy spices are heavily relied on for chili and stews.

Flour tortillas and dairy, like cheddar and Colby jack cheeses, are also major parts of the Tex-Mex food culture, as are queso dips and customizable combinations of rice, beans, proteins, and cheeses in a personal-sized bowl. Or you could just put all those elements together in an oversized burrito. Many of the restaurants on this list do just that, and all of them have been highly rated by fans for taste, price, and overall value. So, the next time you're craving fajitas, quesadillas, and refried beans, feel free to give one of these chains a visit to fulfill that hunger.

Industry observers note that founded in 1991, Mi Cocina is a beloved local chain with just over 20 locations throughout Texas, but the eatery's reputation stretches far further. The upscale Tex-Mex restaurant is just as known for its cocktails, especially the swirled Mambo Taxi Margarita, as it is for the food, such as the fajitas. The upscale brand's dishes include nachos al carbon, poblano chicken enchiladas, and pork picoso tamales that are so flavorful, you definitely won't want to put ketchup on them.

Recent findings suggest that customers rate the restaurant highly on user review platforms, with diners on Yelp saying things like, "Always consistently excellent! My go-to is the brisket tacos and a Dilemma Margarita!" Other guests agree, saying they always enjoy the food when they visit the chain. That reliability is one reason people are so quick to recommend the establishment. Even those who are quite particular about their Tex-Mex fall in love with the place, and many say they'll be back after their first time dining here.

In a recent development, don't make the mistake of confusing Taco Cabana with Taco Bell. Both chains sell tacos, but the smaller restaurant still has a homemade feel, unlike the larger, Tex-Mex fast food super-seller. That's probably because Taco Cabana still makes its from-scratch food from fresh ingredients every day. The differences in flavor and feel in the restaurant's dishes are easy to identify, especially in the handmade flour tortillas. That helps ensure you'll never have to worry about one of the most important elements of a satisfying burrito. And the ones here come overstuffed and covered in optional cheese sauce.

Industry observers note that diners here develop a passion for the chain, or as one TikTok commenter declared, "Taco Cabana is my FAVORITE fast food place. It beats Taco Bell hands down." It's not hard to see why someone might feel that way. Fans enjoy the restaurant's large portions, noting that nachos come in a box large enough to be mistaken for a pizza.

Sources indicate that the meats get their share of the limelight too, with customers recommending items like the beef and chicken fajita nachos, and the customizable protein bowl. One of the brand's latest hit items is the bean and cheese pie, a handheld psuedo-empanada filled with refried beans and yellow cheeses.

According to recent reports, uncle Julio's is an eatery that has understood the importance of making every dish from scratch since it opened several decades ago, and that includes the flour tortillas. Guests are warmly greeted every time they walk through the doors at Moe's Southwest Grill, a tradition the business started at the first location in 2000. The brand is known for innovative flavors and good quality, and customers praise the queso, overstuffed burritos, and customizable bowls, which many say are better than other national brands.

In a recent development, A TikTok user posted about their experience getting a nearly full bag of chips after ordering his mains, and that kind of generosity isn't rare at the chain. Another fan noted how stuffed the birria stack they ordered was, saying it was heavy to pick up, while a first-time diner was impressed by how large the bowl they ordered was.

Fans of Moe's have plenty of choices to customize their bowls and other meals with, but many find their favorite items and stick with them. Or, as one Tripadvisor reviewer said, "... food is splendid! All around just great establishment. We loved everything, especially the queso!!".

Industry observers note that tex-Mex chains are popular and plentiful on the restaurant landscape, so narrowing down this list to the brands fans can't stop raving about took a bit of time. If the restaurants had a focus on flour tortillas, yellow cheeses, and cumin, alongside dishes, like nachos, enchiladas, fajitas, and queso, it qualified as a Tex-Mex establishment.

The eateries had to have more than a dozen locations and good reviews for taste, value, and consistency across multiple sources. The final list was compiled after each chain's specific instances of customer satisfaction were tallied.

Industry News: Add This Ingredient To French Toast For A Crispier Crust (Hint: It's Not Butter Or Oil)

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (624 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A classic French toast recipe is one of those comforting dishes that can be whipped up in a matter of minutes.
  • It has been revealed that semolina is a coarse, pale-yellow flour made by grinding the endosperm of durum wheat, one of the hardest species of wheat there is.
  • Semolina is still flour, so balance is key.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A classic French toast recipe is one of those comforting dishes that can be whipped up in a matter of minutes. However, one common problem people run into is soggy bread rather than a crisp, beautifully caramelized exterior. Unfortunately, sogginess is something of an occupational hazard when you're soaking bread in liquid. To give your slices more of a chance to thrive, all you need to do is add a little semolina flour to your soaking mixture. Two tablespoons per cup and a half of liquid is just about all you need.

It has been revealed that semolina is a coarse, pale-yellow flour made by grinding the endosperm of durum wheat, one of the hardest species of wheat there is. Compared to standard, powdery all-purpose flour, semolina is higher in protein and fiber, and its coarse grains are well-suited to soaking up moisture. In French toast, that can be the difference between a soggy exterior and a crispy one. A small amount turns a watery custard into a more structured batter that clings to the bread instead of letting it drink up all that liquid and fall apart before it even reaches the frying pan. Its subtle nuttiness also adds a whole newly introduced layer of complexity to the flavor of the French toast, and would pair wonderfully with some cosy nutmeg and cinnamon.

Just don't go overboard. Semolina is still flour, so balance is key. Add too little and the mixture stays watery; add too much, and you end up with something closer to a paste than a batter. We recommend starting with a small amount, around a tablespoon, then adjusting until you reach your desired consistency. Semolina flour takes time to absorb liquid, so once you've added it, let the custard sit for a minimum of 10 minutes before adding your bread. Once it's rested, it should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

Industry observers note that semolina is one way to give French toast a crispy, lightly browned exterior, but it's by no means the only one. If you're having a hard time finding it, you can always swap in regular flour. The texture is different, but flour also absorbs liquid and thickens the batter, so you get largely the same effect, just without the nutty flavor. You could even skip the flour altogether and stir a cornstarch slurry into the custard, which packs even more thickening power. Just remember, as with semolina, moderation is key when adding flour or cornstarch into the mix.

Sources indicate that beyond thickening the custard, there are plenty of other handy tricks for shatteringly crispy French toast. To improve both its texture and flavor, give your bread a generous dusting of sugar after it comes out of the custard (before it hits the heat). Alton Brown might prefer honey over sugar in his French toast, but we'd argue that's a rare mistake. See, once sugar hits the heat, it starts to caramelize, melting into a crisp, brûléed crust and infusing the bread with a rich, toasty flavor. Keep the heat moderate, since caramelization can promptly turn to burning without proper care.

If you're not sold on the idea of messing around with the batter or adding extra ingredients, you can guarantee crispy French toast from the get-go by using stale bread. This might not sound too appetizing, but hear us out. Bread that's around one to two days old has lost a good chunk of its moisture, which leaves it firmer and drier. It acts like a sponge, soaking up the custard without turning to mush, so you get a rich, eggy center and a browned exterior instead of a soggy, limp slice.

Industry News: In the Face of Crisis, Psychologists Urge a Return to the Basics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by latest technology, global crises, and loneliness.
  • Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing.
  • Industry observers note that the field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by latest technology, global crises, and loneliness. What do the nation’s psychologists recommend? At the annual convention of the American Psychological Association last month in Washington D.C., that turned out to be a return to the basics: tending to our bodies, connecting in-person, and caring for each other and the most marginalized among us.

In a recent development, joy D. Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing. The chronic stress builds up over time and becomes biological harm, Calloway remarked, citing the weathering theory described by Arline Geronimus, a public health researcher at the University of Michigan. Calloway continued:.

Industry observers note that the field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness. . . . Perhaps our greatest blind spot is that we’ve confused resilience with wellness. . . .

Sources indicate that while wellness begins with individuals, it is nurtured by families, strengthened by communities, and made possible by the systems, institutions, and policies that create the conditions for people to thrive. We don’t simply practice wellness; we build it collectively.

Over three days, nearly 8,000 people from 60 different countries attended the conference in person, participating in a program that included 523 different sessions and 1,180 presenters. The scientific poster program included 91 poster sessions, 2,115 posters, and 1,921 presenters.

In sessions on supporting youth mental health, the impact of technology, and “adulthood unmoored,” APA speakers agreed that many of us are struggling to find purpose and optimism amid technological, climate, and global disruption.

Recent findings suggest that psychologist Ali Mattu noted that over a decade ago, clients sought relief from stress and anxiety, which evolved to seeking relationship and connection support. “Now it’s despair, overwhelm, and meaning,” Mattu told the mainstage audience. “Anyone below the age of 50 here is really searching for meaning, connection, hope, and what do I do with all this overwhelm? What do I do with all of these systems that seem to be collapsing?”.

Perfectionism and the paradox of choice often lie at the root of the overwhelm, noted Thomas Curran, associate professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics. “We don’t worry about what we are doing; we worry about what we could be doing,” Curran said. “It’s like swimming in a vast expanse of ocean with nowhere to dock. It’s frightening, and it feels like no matter what we do, it’s never enough.”.

The answer, Curran said: “Microdose bits of discomfort into daily life.”.

For young people, positive change means pushing back against the ubiquity of technology that purports to connect us but actually keeps us in separate bubbles, staring at our individual feeds. As Nikki Iyer, an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley, framed the problem:.

Our generation might be the most connected generation, but we’re also the loneliest generation. We’re the most alienated generation, and we are desperately craving social connection that we don’t know how to tap. . . . There’s so many people around you all the time. You’re on the train together; you’re in parks; you’re in cafes, but everyone is looking down, and that is a horrific way to grow up as social creatures.

Industry observers note that iyer noted that tech firms wouldn’t be spending such unprecedented amounts of money on lobbying and marketing if they didn’t realize there’s a surge of resistance to artificial intelligence and social media dominating our lives. “The world is in our hands if we are willing to make the leap,” she said, noting a return to “weird” hobbies and in-person activity that replace digital time. “I see a lot of young people pushing back against that.”.

AI models were trained on disproportionately white male–oriented data sets, noted Brendesha Tynes, professor of education and psychology at the University of Southern California’s Rossier School of Education, in urging a slowdown in the adoption of AI.

Recent findings suggest that “Anti-Blackness is the default setting in AI,” Tynes said. Young people need skills “to identify, critique, and cope with the algorithmic bias in technologies that they might witness, and then also to eventually create better AI technologies that don’t have anti-Blackness bias.”.

In sessions across the three days of the conference, researchers presented papers and models for identifying and building on resilience in marginalized communities, from LGBTQ+ youth and adults to disabled and racially marginalized people of all ages.

It has been revealed that joshua Parmenter, an assistant professor at Arizona State University, presented a resistance-resilience model with sexual- and gender-diverse people of color, which involves both individually untangling messages that undermine your well-being and finding collective ways to reclaim power. Jules Soper, a researcher at the Oklahoma State University, offered an investigation of resistance strategies that trans and gender-diverse people use in states that are passing anti-trans legislation.

Industry observers note that alvin Thomas, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, noted that anyone can play a positive role in supporting another member of the community. “I have zero kids, and yet I will still call myself a father. I have nephews; I have nieces; I have kids that I mentor from across the Caribbean and across the U.S.,” Thomas said.

Clare M. Mehta, professor of psychology at Emmanuel College and visiting researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, encouraged everyone to look for ways to be a “villager” who reaches out to another person, and seeks out connection in third spaces. She continued:.

In a recent development, we have to start going back to the pub again. People have been concerned for years and years that drinking alcohol is bad for your health, but not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. . . . You don’t have to drink alcohol at the pub. They serve other drinks, right? Go and have a glass of orange juice or like a fizzy water. Not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health.

Young people actually are wired to be a positive force for change, noted Eva Telzer, professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Recent findings suggest that “Young people are superhuman in the way their brains are set up to be risk takers but also to care about others, for peers, and for social interactions to be so important,” Telzer said in a question-and-answer period after her mainstage remarks. “That puts them in this perfect place to make change and do good in the world.”.

Even technology has a role to play, Mattu noted. “AI should be a co-intelligence that enhances the things we are very bad at,” he said, urging people to take the opportunity to define clearly the uniquely human pursuits we should claim, and in which domains technology is appropriate to be a useful aid.

He suggested three criteria for the activities to avoid replacing with AI: what you love, what you have expertise in, and what you hold high standards for. As Jacqueline S. Mattis, a psychologist and dean at Rutgers University, Newark, told her audience:.

Industry observers note that we start as this passel of cells, and then we end up laughing, and that’s amazing. You get to experience the magnificence of being able to feel affection for another human being, so much so that you will sacrifice everything for them. That’s amazing. . . . All of that is what defines us as truly human and defines this thing called life as worth living.

Katherine Reynolds Lewis is the special projects editor at the Greater Good Science Center and author of the Good News About Bad Behavior. She is an award-winning science journalist with bylines in the Atlantic, Fortune, New York Times, Undark, and Washington Post.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Chili is one of those meals that scratches an itch that no other comfort food can quite compare to. You can go with beans or no beans, or even make a super satisfying vegan version. A big batch can be pretty easy to make in the slow cooker, but despite the simple prep, it still takes a lot of time. So, when you want a quick hit, you can always reach for your favorite brand of the canned stuff. However, there's an easy trick to up the flavor of your meal — add a dash of instant coffee. The incredible blend of flavors might just blow your mind.

Instant coffee crystals will add some bold, roasted richness to your chili. Sure, coffee is bitter, but if you don't go overboard, its presence will be subtle, making your chili taste more like something homemade that's been simmering on the stove all day. It creates a nice depth by enhancing the perception of the beefy umami and highlighting spices like cumin, coriander, cayenne, and chili powder. It can also help offset some of the perceived acidity in the tomato-heavy sauce, giving you an end result that's more balanced on the palate and beautifully tied together.

If you don't already have instant coffee in the pantry, instant espresso, like Medaglia D'Oro Instant Espresso, is sometimes preferred because it dissolves more easily, but really, any instant coffee will work. Just keep in mind that espresso will have a stronger flavor, and the strength of any given coffee crystals can vary a bit. Start with just a pinch, or about a ¼ teaspoon per 15-ounce can of chili. You can dissolve it in a few spoonfuls of hot water first to ensure it doesn't clump, but if the chili is already simmering, it should blend in easily, especially in small amounts. Give it a taste and add more if you'd like.

If you want to go for bolder undertones, a touch of cocoa powder pairs nicely with coffee crystals. If you want to skip the instant coffee and use the real thing, you can add a little brewed coffee or finely ground espresso (but when using the latter, you'll need to mix it into a paste with some water so you don't end up with a mouthful of grounds). A splash of bourbon, or even beer, can help round out the flavor with the coffee. And much like it works in chili, instant coffee can wake up your spaghetti sauce. But to get that great earthy, bold flavor in a full meal right off the shelf, you're going to want to try coffee crystals in your canned chili.

At first glance, tuna salad may appear to be a fairly set-in-stone formula. You mix the tinned fish with mayo, add in some aromatics, and enjoy the dish on bread or standalone. Yet start trialing creative add-ins, and tuna salad welcomes a surprisingly wide array of ingredients. There are so many ways to take plain tuna salad to the next level. A sharp cheddar cheese is one unexpected flavor boost.

After all, creaminess is a central part of the dish's appeal. And as a dairy product, cheddar cheese offers such a smooth mouthfeel in spades. However, unlike a simple mayo dressing, the cheese comes with a punch. Aging develops complex flavors, which can vary from barely perceptible tartness to rich nuttiness to a bold bite. Usually, the older the cheddar, the more amplified the flavor — although as the cheese develops, it loses some creaminess to become crumbly.

For a top-tier cheddar tuna salad, go with a balanced option, aged for around six to nine months. Usually classified specifically as sharp, such a cheese is right when the acidic flavors turn into a bold bite — perfect for a tuna salad. So cube up the cheese, using two ounces per can of tuna, then stir everything up with some salt, onions, celery, and your other go-to tuna salad fold-ins. You'll get a dish that's still comforting, but also comes with revamped flair.

It has been revealed that as America's favorite cheese, cheddar certainly belongs in a dish like tuna salad. While it's not common to mix cheese directly into the salad, the inclusion is reminiscent of a beloved tuna salad application: a tuna melt. Originating by mistake, the tuna melt proves that fish and cheese do belong on the same plate, especially if tuna's involved.

In a recent development, further embrace the two dishes by heating the cheddar cheese tuna salad. The cheese will turn molten inside — not only on top — of the fish, making for an extra-satisfying filling. Pair that with a nice bread, say a classic American white loaf, a deli-inspired rye, or a dependable sourdough, and you've got a terrific sandwich on your hands.

Not to say there's not more magic to explore with a cold cheddar tuna salad, too. The cheesy rendition is a befitting tuna pasta salad twist. Or balance out cheddar's richness by rolling the salad into lettuce wraps, a delicious appetizer option. Cheddar gives tuna salad that extra oomph, turning the basic dish into a centerpiece meal.

Skip The Pan: Grilled Cheese Is 10x Crispier When You Cook It Like This

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you like it on its own or coupled with a bowl of roasted tomato soup, a grilled cheese is one of life's simple pleasures.
  • Industry observers note that this technique mimics a panini press, which functions by heating top and bottom metal plates connected by a hinge.
  • The oven also has the advantage of providing ambient heat since it's an enclosed environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you like it on its own or coupled with a bowl of roasted tomato soup, a grilled cheese is one of life's simple pleasures. Making one for yourself is simple enough in a pan or skillet. However, preparing half a dozen or more can be a pretty significant undertaking on the stovetop. Fortunately, there's an easier way. By using a couple of baking sheets and your oven, you can conveniently whip up a large batch of these cheesy sandwiches that come out super crispy.

Industry observers note that this technique mimics a panini press, which functions by heating top and bottom metal plates connected by a hinge. This gets both sides of the sandwich crispy at the same time, eliminating the need for flipping. However, these presses have their downsides. The weight of the plates, for instance, can turn softer bread into a pancake. Baking sheets, on the other hand, are much lighter and won't compromise the integrity of more delicate breads.

The oven also has the advantage of providing ambient heat since it's an enclosed environment. This means that your sandwich is getting heated on all sides instead of just the top and bottom, helping to create crisp crusts and melted cheese. However, you still need to preheat your top baking sheet for even crispness, since the bottom of your sandwiches could brown before the tops get crispy.

Sources indicate that depending on how many sandwiches you want to prepare, you can vary the size of the baking sheet you use. To make about six to eight at once, use a half-sheet pan, which measures about 18 inches by 13 inches and is probably the size you have at home. You can also use a quarter-sheet pan if you want to make fewer.

Sources indicate that while the fat you spread on your bread (we recommend mayo for the crispiest results) will help ensure that your sandwiches don't stick to the baking sheets, you can also take a tip from Ina Garten and use parchment paper to line the pans for extra insurance. Also, don't stick to just using your baking sheets right side up. In fact, using your bottom pan upside down will allow for more airflow since the rim won't get in the way, thus crisping your sandwiches more effectively.

To make this technique really work, though, you're going to need to make sure you choose the right kind of cheese that will melt easily by the time the crusts of your sandwiches become golden brown. After all, you don't want to have to keep putting your grilled cheeses back in the oven to finish melting. The best options have a good balance of moisture and fat, and younger cheeses tend to be the go-to varieties that meet this standard. Some recommendations include Havarti, Gruyère, and cheddar. However, you can opt for some underrated (but tasty) cheeses to give your sandwiches extra character. You can also combine several types of cheese for a more varied flavor and texture.

#92103. Can Consciousness Exist Without a Body?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2384 w)
